QUESTIONS PRESENTED

2. Whether the district court had authority to enter

U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1).
3.  Whether the Government’s Guidance on third -
country removals is unlawful under 8 U.S.C. § 1231(b), the

(1)
In the Supreme Court of the United States
_____________
No. 26-426
DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY, ET AL.,
PETITIONERS
v.
D.V.D., ET AL., RESPONDENTS
_____________
ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE FIRST CIRCUIT
_____________
BRIEF OF PROFESSOR PHILIP HAMBURGER AND
THE NEW CIVIL LIBERTIES ALLIANCE AS
AMICI  CURIAE  IN SUPPORT OF NEITHER PARTY 1
_____________
What does the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”)
mean when its Section 706 requires a court to “set aside”
unlawful or unauthorized agency actions? Is it speaking of
a remedy — indeed, an injunction or other equitable remedy — against a party? Or is it instead echoing the super-
1. No counsel for a party authored any part of this brief. And no one
other than amici curiae, their members, or their counsel financed
the preparation or submission of this brief.

2
visory power of appellate courts over lower courts, attributing to an appellate court a power to supervise agencies
in the same manner that it ordinarily would supervise
lower courts? This amici curiae brief will address these
questions to answer the second Question Presented, as
added by the Court when it granted certiorari in this case.
The Solicitor General’s office,2 as well as some scholars
and members of this Court,3 say that the duty of courts to
“set aside” unlawful agency action is a remedy akin to an
injunction — a universal injunction even— thus subjecting
it to all the limits on equitable remedies and tarring it with
all that seems wrong with universal injunctions. These critiques might, possibly , seem to make sense if “setting
aside” really were a sort of equitable remedy or universal
injunction.
But a statute authorizing reviewing courts to “set
aside” unlawful “agency action” does not deploy the language of equitable remedies directed at parties. Rather ,
2. Pet. Br. 29 n.5; Pet. at 11–24, Department of Health and Human
Services v. Texas Medical Association, No. 26-491 (filed Oct. 14,
2026).
3. See John Harrison, Section 706 of the Administrative Procedure
Act Does Not Call for Universal Injunctions or Other Universal
Remedies, 37 Yale J. on Reg. Bull. 37 (2020); John Harrison, Vacatur of Rules Under the Administrative Procedure Act, 40 Yale
J. on Reg. Bull. 119 (2023); United States v. Texas, 599 U.S. 670,
693–704 (2023) (Gorsuch, J., concurring in the judgment); But see
T. Elliot Gaiser, Mathura Sridharan & Nicholas Cordova, The
Truth of Erasure: Universal Remedies for Universal Agency Actions, U. Chi. L. Rev. Online (Aug. 28, 2024) , https://lawreview.
uchicago.edu/online-archive/truth-erasure-universal-remediesuniversal-agency-actions [https://perma.cc/62VAP54B] (arguing
that Prof. Harrison’ s interpretation of Section 706’s ‘set aside’
language is “implausible”).

3
the phrase “set aside,” as used in the APA, is borrowed
from and refers to the practice of courts reviewing judgments—either their own judgments or those of other
courts. Once that is recognized, it becomes clear that
courts have not only the power but also the duty to set
aside agency actions to the extent they are unauthorized
or otherwise unlawful. Indeed, the formal vacatur of an
unauthorized or otherwise unlawful agency action is necessary to protect constitutional freedoms and Congress’s
role as legislator.
INTEREST OF AMICI
Philip Hamburger is the Maurice and Hilda Friedman
Professor of Law at Columbia Law School and an historian of constitutional law . His Law and Judicial Duty
(Harvard Univ . 2008) showed that early Americans understood judges to have an office, or duty , of independent
judgment in accord with the law of the land—this being
the foundation for what long afterward came to be called
judicial review. In his book Is Administrative Law Unlawful? (Univ . of Chicago 2014), Hamburger traced the
development of administrative power. He showed that administrative power consists of irregular legislative and judicial pathways that evade the Constitution’s regular avenues of power and that the Constitution was framed to bar
such evasions. He is deeply concerned that the Solicitor
General’s misinterpretation of APA Section 706 would encourage unconstitutional agency action and would cripple
the ability of Americans to protect their constitutional
freedoms.

4
The New Civil Liberties Alliance (NCLA) is a nonprofit, public-interest law firm founded to challenge multiple constitutional defects in the modern administrative
state through original litigation, amicus curiae briefs,
and other means. The “civil liberties” of the organization’s
name include rights at least as old as the U.S. Constitution
itself, such as jury trial, due process of law , the right to be
tried in front of an impartial and independent judge, and
the right to have laws made by the nation’s elected lawmakers through constitutionally prescribed channels rather than executive-branch officials acting outside those
channels. Y et these selfsame civil rights are also very contemporary—and in dire need of renewed vindication—
precisely because federal administrative agencies have
trampled them for so long.
NCLA aims to defend civil liberties primarily by asserting constitutional constraints on the administrative
state. Although Americans still enjoy the shell of their Republic, there has developed within it a very different sort
of government—a type, in fact, that the Constitution was
designed to prevent. This unconstitutional state within
the Constitution’s United States is the focus of NCLA’s
concern.
NCLA takes no position on the jurisdictional or constitutional due-process arguments that appear in the Solicitor General’s brief. NCLA ’s interest in this litigation
arises from the Solicitor General’s misguided insistence
that the phrase “set aside” in Section 706 of the APA cannot authorize universal vacatur of “agency action.” Pet.
Br. 29 n.5. The Solicitor General has asked the Court not
to resolve the meaning of “set aside” in this litigation, and

5
NCLA agrees with the Solicitor General that it would be
ill advised for this Court to weigh in when the parties have
not locked horns on the issue. But NCLA nonetheless
wishes to dispel the notion that the APA forbids courts to
formally vacate agency rules—as this revisionist understanding of Section 706 is gaining traction in academic and
judicial circles. See Harrison, supra; Texas, 599 U.S. at
693–704 (Gorsuch, J., concurring in the judgment); Life-
Link Found., Inc. v. Kennedy, No. 8:25-cv-2042, 2026 WL
2914221 (M.D. Fla. Sept. 29, 2026).
CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY
PROVISIONS INVOL VED
5 U.S.C. § 706 provides, in relevant part:
The reviewing court shall—
(1) compel agency action unlawfully withheld or
unreasonably delayed; and
(2) hold unlawful and set aside agency action,
findings, and conclusions found to be—
(A) arbitrary , capricious, an abuse of discretion,
or otherwise not in accordance with law;
(B) contrary to constitutional right, power, privilege, or immunity;
(C) in excess of statutory jurisdiction, authority ,
or limitations, or short of statutory right;
(D) without observance of procedure required
by law;

6
(E) unsupported by substantial evidence in a
case subject to sections 556 and 557of this title
or otherwise reviewed on the record of an
agency hearing provided by statute; or
(F) unwarranted by the facts to the extent that
the facts are subject to trial de novo by the reviewing court.
ARGUMENT
I. CONGRESS ADOPTED A JUDICIAL MODEL OF
AGENCIES, BY WHICH THEIR RULES ARE
REVIEWED IN THE MANNER OF TRIAL COURTS’
JUDGMENTS
The APA ’s use of the phrase “set aside” draws upon
familiar language about the power of appellate courts to
“set aside” or “vacate” the action of a lower court, thereby
giving appellate courts a similar power over administrative agencies. This is clear from the language and context
of 5 U.S.C. § 706.
The relationship between appellate courts and trial
courts served as the model for the courts’ relationship to
federal agencies. This judicial model has been the foundation of federal administrative structures since the early
twentieth century . See Thomas W . Merrill, Article III,
Agency Adjudication, and the Origins of the Appellate
Review Model of Administrative Law, 111 Colum. L. Rev .
939, 940 (2011) (explaining how judicial review of agency
action is “built on the appellate review model of the relationship between reviewing courts and agencies,” which
“was borrowed from the understandings that govern the
relationship between appeals courts and trial courts in

7
civil litigation”); Nicholas Bagley , Remedial Restraint in
Administrative Law, 117 Colum. L. Rev . 253, 258 (2017)
(“The APA instructs federal courts to ‘hold unlawful and
set aside’ arbitrary or unlawful agency action. When the
APA was enacted in 1946, that instruction reflected a consensus that judicial review of agency action should be
modeled on appellate review of trial court judgments … .
Just as a district court judgment infected with error
should be invalidated and returned for reconsideration, so
too with agency action.” (footnotes omitted)). Congress
adopted this model in Section 706 of the APA, and it remains the key to understanding that section’s phrase “set
aside.”
From 1887 onward, Congress authorized one commission after another to hold hearings in a judicial manner.
On the basis of these hearings, the commissions both
made rules and adjudicated—in what came to be known
as “formal rulemaking” and “formal adjudication.” This
judicial model of agency proceedings, which included the
sorts of activities otherwise done in Congress and the
courts, became the basis for courts to review agency actions in a manner similar to an appellate court’s review of
trial-court proceedings.
The early decisions of the Supreme Court in this area
recognized this judicial model of federal agencies. As the
Court summarized in the syllabus of one of its cases, relied upon here for historical description, not as matter of
law: “The Act to Regulate Commerce, as amended by the
Hepburn Act, gives a right to a full hearing on the subject
of rates, and that confers the privilege of introducing testimony and imposes the duty of deciding in accordance

8
with the facts proved.” Interstate Com. Comm’n v. Louisville & Nash. R.R. Co., 227 U.S. 88, 88 (1913). The Court
added that these agency hearings were reviewable in a
structure akin to an appellate court’s review of trial-court
proceedings: “ Administrative orders quasi-judicial in
character are void if a hearing is denied; if the hearing
granted is manifestly unfair, if the finding is indisputably
contrary to the evidence, or if the facts found do not, as
matter of law , support the order made.” Id.
John Dickinson’s 1927 treatise explains that the judicial model of agencies, including the power of courts to set
aside (i.e., formally vacate) their decisions as if they were
jury verdicts, was essential to preserving the supremacy
of law and thus the legitimacy of the administrative state:
“The door through which a way is properly opened for judicial interference with administrative application  of
standards is the well-established doctrine that a determination will be set aside which is without evidence to support it. This is a rule obviously borrowed from the law governing court control of the verdicts of juries.” John Dickinson, Administrative Justice and the Supremacy of Law
in the United States 320 (1927).
The Attorney General’s 1941 Report on Administrative Procedure in Government Agencies, which laid the
foundation for the APA, likewise recognizes the judicial
model. It explains that regulation, not just adjudication,
took the form of a trial, subject to judicial review: “Some
of the recent statutes conferring rule-making power …
require that the regulations in question be based upon
findings of fact; that these, in turn, be based upon evidence made of record at a hearing; and that a reviewing

9
court set aside a regulation not only for failure of the findings to support it, but also for failure of a finding to be
based upon substantial evidence in the record.” Attorney
General’s Committee on Administrative Procedure, U.S.
Dep’t of Justice, Administrative Procedure in Government Agencies 116–17 (1941) [hereinafter “Report”]. After certification of the administrative record to the court,
“[a] judgment adverse to a regulation results in setting it
aside.” Id. at 117.
This was a “novel type of judicial review” because it
dealt with “regulations,” not “an ordinary trial.” Id. The
key point is that it treated regulation-making like the decision of a trial court, which could be set aside (i.e., formally vacated) on review by a higher court.
Section 706—the APA’s provision authorizing judicial
review of agency action, which includes the phrase “set
aside”—clearly built upon this judicial model. That section concludes: “In making the foregoing determinations,
the court shall review the whole record or those parts of it
cited by a party … .” This spells out that the agency is
being treated like a trial court, which develops a record
subject to review by a higher court.
The Committee’s Report, as might be expected, objected to suggestions that an agency should be subject to
the same standard of review as a trial court: “Judicial review of administrative decisions might be expanded to include a review of the findings in the light of the weight of
the evidence, just as a trial judge may set aside a jury’s
verdict on this ground . . . . but the plan is unquestionably
against the present trend of administrative legislation …

10
.” Report 250. Agencies were to be reviewed like courts,
but not so rigorously .
This vision of agencies as if they were courts is apparent through much of the APA, including its requirements
of finality and exhaustion. Section 704 restricts judicial review to “final agency action for which there is no other adequate remedy in a court” and requires exhaustion of
agency remedies. Similar is the tendency of appellate
courts to “remand” proceeding to agencies. Agencies are
thus treated like lower courts, not like parties.
In this context, when Section 706 requires reviewing
courts to “hold unlawful and set aside agency action, findings, and conclusions,” it clearly is speaking about setting
aside an agency’s action as if it were a lower court. Tellingly , this setting aside is required when the agency action
is found to have failings akin to those of trial courts:
(A) arbitrary , capricious, an abuse of discretion,
or otherwise not in accordance with law;
(B) contrary to constitutional right, power, privilege, or immunity;
(C) in excess of statutory jurisdiction, authority ,
or limitations, or short of statutory right;
(D) without observance of procedure required
by law;
(E) unsupported by substantial evidence in a
case subject to sections 556 and 557 of this title
or otherwise reviewed on the record of an
agency hearing provided by statute; or

11
(F) unwarranted by the facts to the extent that
the facts are subject to trial de novo by the reviewing court.
5 U.S.C. § 706. These categories are not all exactly the errors of trial courts, but even where they deviate from the
traditional errors of trial courts, they are the sort of errors that justify appellate courts reversing and setting
aside (i.e., formally vacating) the decisions of trial courts.
Setting aside is part of the judicial model, in which appellate courts treat agencies roughly like trial courts.
Of course, it is open to doubt whether this treatment
of agencies as if they were courts is fully constitutional.
The validity of vacatur, however, is a different question.
The Solicitor General argues that Section 706’s use of the
phrase “set aside” refers to injunctions or something analogous to injunctions against a party . But federal law from
the early twentieth century through the present, including Section 706, gave appellate courts the sort of supervisory power over agencies that these courts ordinarily
wielded over trial courts. Section 706’s words “set aside”
are therefore inescapably part of the judicial model of
agencies and any attempts to deny this framework wrest
those words out of the context that throughout the twentieth century was assumed to legitimize administrative
power.
II. UNDER THE APA, COURTS HAVE A DUTY TO
“SET ASIDE” AGENCY ACTION IN THE SAME
WAY THAT THEY SET ASIDE LOWER-COURT
DECISIONS
As one might expect from the judicial model of agencies, the phrase “set aside” in Section 706 mean s the

12
power of a court to set aside, or vacate, the act of an
agency in the same manner that an appellate court could
set aside, or vacate, the action of a lower court. It has been
suggested by academics and the Solicitor General that
those words are ambiguous or that they mean something
akin to an injunction or other remedy directed at parties.
But those words had a very different meaning in treatises
and countless judicial decisions on the supervisory power
of courts over other courts, and Section 706’s phrase “set
aside” must be read in light of that conventional meaning.
Dictionaries make clear that to “vacate” or “set aside”
was typically to annul or hold void a legal proceeding or
decision. Kinney’s Law Dictionary said that to “set aside”
was primarily “[t]o annul, make void or vacate,” and similarly “vacatur” was “a rule or an order by which a proceeding is vacated.” J. Kendrick Kinney , A Law Dictionary and Glossary 620, 677 (1893). Bouvier’s Law Dictionary explained that to “vacate” was to “annul; to render an
act void: as, to vacate an entry which has been made on a
record . . .” and that to “set aside” was “to make void: as,
to set aside an award.” Vacate, Bouvier’s Law Dictionary:
Student Edition (1928); set aside, Bouvier’s Law Dictionary. Black’s Law Dictionary similarly observed: “To set
aside a judgment, decree, award, or any proceedings is to
cancel, annul, or revoke them.” See set aside, Black’s Law
Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910), https://blackslaw .io/.
The term “set aside” could be used interchangeably
with “vacate,” “annul,” and “reverse” to refer to the supervisory power of an appellate court to hold another
court’s judgment void. See, e.g., 1 Henry Campbell Black,
A Treatise on the Law of Judgments 408 (1891); see also

13
A.C. Freeman, A Treatise on the Law of Judgments 590
(5th ed. 1925) (“The power to vacate a judgment carries
with it the power to set aside the verdict on which it was
founded”); id. at 616 (“suits seeking to set aside or annul
judgments”); id. at 1407 (“subsequent proceedings to vacate or set aside the judgment”); id.at 1524 (“reversed or
set aside”).
Often these terms were used together, as if for emphasis, as in to “set aside and vacate” or to “vacate and set
aside.” A search in Google Books for the first phrase in
publications appearing from 1930 to 1950 has about 3,400
results.4 The second produces about 15,200 results.5 Overwhelmingly , the prevailing context is an appellate court
vacating or setting aside the judgment or other action of
a court.
A court could set aside its own judgments, as “[a]ll
judgments, decrees or other orders of a court are under
its control during the term and may be set aside, vacated,
modified or annulled by it.” Freeman, Judgments at 377.
A court could also set aside the judgments of courts subject to its supervision—this being part of the court’s supervisory power over another court.
Until a court’s judgment was reversed or set aside, the
judgment remained binding. 2 Henry Campbell Black, A
Treatise on the Law of Judgments 709 (1891) (“Like any
other adjudication, a judgment against a garnishee, no

4. Google Books, “set aside and vacate” (Oct. 26, 2026),
https://bit.ly/4jM8omr.
5. Google Books, “vacate and set aside” (Oct. 26, 2026),
https://bit.ly/4zkBbTY.

14
matter how erroneous, is final and binding until it is reversed or set aside.”). Once the judgment was set aside or
reversed, however, it was void, in the sense of devoid of
obligation.
The judgment that another court’s judgment was to be
set aside was distinct from any injunctive or equitable
remedy , and lawyers understood this: “Quite generally
bills and complaints to set aside or impeach the judgment”
are “accompanied … with a prayer that its enforcement
be enjoined.” Freeman, Judgments at 613–14. Setting
aside a judgment and enjoining its enforcement were different. Similarly , it was said that “even an inequitable
judgment will not be set aside nor will its enforcement be
enjoined where it was the result of the complaining
party’s fault or inexcusable neglect.” Id. at 2500.
To be sure, proceedings to set aside the judgment of
another court were sometime loosely said to be “equitable,” in sense that they were to secure justice, but they
were not equitable in the sense of being within equitable
jurisdiction or involving an equitable remedy . Speaking of
the proceedings of a court to vacate its own judgments,
Freeman explained: “While proceedings to set aside judgments are often regarded as equitable in their nature, unless they are actually or in legal effect suits in equity , they
are not governed by the equitable rule that the existence
of another adequate remedy bars the right to relief. If the
statute gives the right to have a judgment vacated under
given conditions, the fact that there may be a concurrent
remedy by appeal or otherwise is immaterial.” Freeman,
Judgments at 402 (footnotes omitted). To “set aside” was

15
to annul the action of a court, not to grant an injunction or
other equitable remedy .
There is no reason to think that the APA abandoned
the conventional and dominant understanding of “set
aside.” The APA’s statement that courts shall “set aside”
unlawful action was phrased in the familiar language that
almost all courts, state and federal, used in reviewing the
actions of other courts. Section 706 adopted that phrase
within its judicial model of agencies—treating them as if
they were lower courts for purposes of review—and it did
so without disclaiming the conventional and dominant usage. In light of that prevailing usage and the judicial
model of agencies, no one in drafting or adopting the APA
could have been in any doubt about the meaning of “set
aside.”
To “set aside” an agency action had the same import
as to “set aside” a court decision. Setting aside was an utterly familiar part of the ordinary supervisory power of
courts over the judicial system, not a remedy , let alone an
injunctive or other equitable remedy . Not merely an academic theory , or the product of selective evidence, this
meaning of “set aside” was familiar throughout the federal and state court systems, including for reviewing
agency actions. So, when the APA adopted the phrase “set
aside” in its judicial-review section, it clearly required a
court in reviewing the action of an agency to set it aside in
the same way , and to the same extent, as it would set aside
the decision of a lower court.

16
III. SETTING ASIDE IS SUPERVISORY , NOT
INJUNCTIVE OR OTHERWISE REMEDIAL
The history of statutes authorizing judicial review of
agencies clearly shows that to “set aside” an agency action
was part of the appellate review of agencies, not a remedy
available for one party against another. The scholarship of
Professor Emily Bremer already argues that “vacatur is
not an equitable remedy but an appellate determination.”
Emily S. Bremer, Vacatur Within the Appellate Model of
Judicial Review, 136 Y ale L.J. (forthcoming 2026), available at https://perma.cc/J738-NP35. And even clearer evidence of that point can be found in the contrast between
the two leading types of authorizing statutes.
The statutes authorizing district-court review authorized both enjoining and setting aside agency action. The
statutes authorizing appellate review of agency action authorized only setting aside, not injunctions. The APA
adopted the latter approach.
The Attorney General’s Report on Administrative
Procedure in Government Agencies (1941) already recognized the difference between these two lines of statutes.
Discussing appeals to district courts, the Report observed
that “the Hepburn Act in 1906 conferred jurisdiction on
the Federal district courts to ‘enjoin, set aside, or annul’
orders of the Interstate Commerce Commission.” Report
at 82. The Report then explained that appellate-court review had come to seem preferable: “ A method of review
which has found considerable favor in recent legislation is
that first enacted in the Federal Trade Commission Act in

17
1914, that is, review in a Circuit Court of Appeals with discretionary appellate jurisdiction in the Supreme Court.”
Id. at 83.
This appellate review , initiated by the Federal Trade
Commission Act and given effect by a long line of statutes,
dropped the word “enjoin” and, instead, merely authorized a circuit court to “set aside” or otherwise adjust
agency action. The 1914 statute authorized circuit courts
merely “to affirm, set aside, or modify the order of the
commission.” Federal Trade Commission Act, ch. 311, 38
Stat. 717, 720 (1914). Similarly , for example, the Securities
Exchange Act of 1934 provided that the courts of appeals
“shall have exclusive jurisdiction to affirm, modify , and enforce or set aside such order, in whole or in part.” Securities Exchange Act of 1934, ch. 404, § 25(a), 48 Stat. 881,
902. The National Labor Relations Act of 1935 (Wagner
Act) similarly authorized courts of appeals “to make and
enter a decree enforcing, modifying, and enforcing as so
modified, or setting aside in whole or in part the order of
the Board.” National Labor Relations Act of 1935, ch. 372,
§ 10(f), 49 Stat. 449, 453–55. The Investment Company
Act of 1940 and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 authorized appellate courts “to affirm, modify , or set aside.”
Investment Company Act of 1940, ch. 686, § 43(a), 54 Stat.
789, 844; Investment Advisers Act of 1940, ch. 686,
§ 213(a), 54 Stat. 847, 855.
There were thus two lines of statutes, one giving district courts power to “enjoin” and to “set aside” etc., the
other giving appellate courts power merely to “set aside”
and so forth. The APA, as anticipated by the Attorney
General’s Report, adopted the appellate model of review

18
and its limitation of the courts to supervising agencies as
if they were trial courts.
The remedial vision of setting aside, which would have
this court imagine it is issuing an injunction against a
party , collides with the overwhelming evidence that to “set
aside” is part of the appellate supervision of agencies as if
they were lower courts. Not a remedy , let alone an injunction, the power to “set aside” is the supervisory power to
vacate lower court or agency action.
Of course, even when agencies were treated as trial
courts, they remained parties to the proceeding—a constitutional conundrum that still looks incongruous. The
district-court-review statutes therefore treated agencies
as ambidextrous—authorizing both injunctions against
them as parties and the setting aside of their actions as if
they were lower courts. The APA, however, in adopting
the appellate-court approach, merely authorized setting
aside. In other words, it confined itself to the judicial
model of agencies, not the party model of agencies.
A court must therefore set aside agency action without
regard to equitable defenses and other concerns about
remedies. Setting aside is not an injunction or other remedy , and to conflate this supervisory authority of appellate
courts with injunctive remedies against parties is more
than mere confusion; it is a category error.
IV. DISTRICT COURTS HAVE GREATER POWER
REGARDING AGENCY RULES THAN THEY DO
OVER STATUTES
It makes perfect sense that Congress would give federal district courts the ability to “set aside” unlawful
agency rules under Section 706, even if one does not think

19
that district courts have (or should have) the ability to set
aside unlawful federal statutes. A statute typically arrives
in federal court having gone through both houses of Congress and having obtained the President’s signature. That
is, it has gone through the constitutionally prescribed processes for creating law that binds the populace, which
means that two separate elected branches of the federal
government have already , at least implicitly , determined
that the law is constitutional. So it is for good reason that
a presumption of constitutionality attaches to a statute
that is being challenged before a federal district court.
By contrast, in order for a rule to be published in the
Federal Register, it does not go through either house of
Congress, so the legislative branch has not necessarily
blessed it at all. In terms of the executive branch, the
President does not sign off on rules. Sometimes the secretary of the agency has not signed off on the rule. Sometimes not even the general counsel of the agency has
signed off on the rule.  It is not required for a rule to be
published in the Federal Register that it have been signed
off on by the head of the agency .6 It is more a matter of
what the internal rules are at the particular agency or department as to who has to sign off on it before it goes into

150 Daedalus 220, 228 (2021) (“Faced with a significant volume of
regulatory responsibility, agency heads sometimes subdelegate
their statutory authority, with varying degrees of residual oversight. Agency staff can thus seize the opportunity to identify a
problem and write up an advanced notice of proposed rulemaking, then a notice of proposed rulemaking, and ultimately a final
rule. Depending on the agency and its organization, and the importance of the regulation, such activity might be reviewed by
senior officials[.]”)

20
the Federal Register. In a big cabinet agency like the Department of Health and Human Services, for example,
there are rules that get into the Federal Register all the
time that the Secretary of HHS has not signed off on.
Even fairly low-level, unelected bureaucrats sometimes
have the power to promulgate regulations. For these reasons, no presumption of constitutionality attaches to an
agency rule that is being challenged before a federal district court, and judges should not hesitate to set them
aside when they are unlawful.
So, what happens when a rule reaches the federal district court and there is a person in court who has been injured by that rule, and that person claims that the rule is
unconstitutional, or that the agency lacked statutory authority to promulgate it? That federal district court judge
is potentially the first federal constitutional officer who
has looked at this question in an independent way to determine whether this rule is lawful or not. If that judge
decides that this rule was done without statutory authority or in violation of the constitution or in some procedurally defective or other unlawful way , the judge has a duty
to set aside that rule. A judge who does so is not overcoming the will of at least half of Congress and an elected
President. Rather, the judge might well be countermanding a single unelected bureaucrat—and standing up for
the will of Congress at the same time.
It is not surprising then that Section 706 gave federal
district judges the ability to set aside rules. Rules are not
statutes. They do not have the imprimatur of the elected
legislative branch nor the approval of the highest executive branch official. Administrative rulemaking is not

21
mentioned in the Constitution at all and it lacks the difficult-to-satisfy front-end constraints on lawmaking, so it is
already of dubious provenance. To constrain the administrative state at all and to lend legitimacy to agency rulemaking, strong judicial review must remain as a backstop.
District judges must have the whip hand to stop unauthorized or otherwise unlawful agency action. Otherwise, the
Executive Branch will be able to outrun the courts. Congress gave district judges the power to set aside rules so
that they would be able to police agencies that might otherwise get away with ignoring the will of Congress.7
V. APPELLATE COURTS HAVE THE
CONSTITUTIONAL AUTHORITY AND DUTY TO
SET ASIDE AGENCY ACTION TO THE EXTENT IT
IS UNLAWFUL, WITHOUT INTERFERENCE
FROM THE POLITICAL BRANCHES
The judicial power that the Constitution vests in the
courts is accompanied by the judicial duty of each judge
to exercise independent judgment in accord with the
law—this being the heart of judicial office. See Philip
Hamburger, Law and Judicial Duty (2008). Accordingly ,
when a judge reaches the conclusion that an agency action
is unlawful, he has not only the power but also the duty to
set it aside to the extent it is unlawful. This setting aside

Truth of Erasure: Universal Remedies for Universal Agency Actions, U. Chi. L. Rev. Online (Aug. 28, 2024) (“If courts could not
universally vacate agency action that unlawfully regulates with
universal effect, then the Constitution’s allocation of powers
would be distorted by executive branch ‘lawmakers’ insufficiently

22
of unlawful agency action is thus not merely a requirement of the APA; nor is the extent of setting aside left to
the discretion of the judges. Instead, setting aside agency
action, to the degree it is unlawful, is the natural and required consequence of finding such action unlawful. This
is inherent in judicial power and duty , and Section 706 of
the APA recognizes this duty by saying: “The reviewing
court shall … hold unlawful and set aside agency action,
findings, and conclusions found to be … arbitrary , capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law … .” 5 U.S.C. § 706 (emphasis added).
The Solicitor General suggests that only Congress or
the agency itself can alter agency rules. But the judicial
authority to set aside unlawful acts of lower courts or
agencies is part of the judicial power, not a legislative or
executive power, and it therefore cannot be confined by
the political branches. Freeman explained:
The power to vacate or set aside judgments and
decrees, must be exercised solely by the judiciary . The legislature cannot set aside a judgment,
nor can it empower any court to set aside a judgment which had been rendered and had passed
beyond the control of the court prior the passage of the act; because in so doing the legislature is exercising judicial functions not accorded
to it by the constitution . . .
Freeman, Judgments 395. From this perspective, it must
be doubted whether, once Congress has given the courts
jurisdiction over agencies, it can restrict a court from setting aside an unlawful agency action.

23
VI. FORMAL VA CAT U R OF UNLAWFUL AGENCY
ACTION IS CRUCIAL TO PROTECT
CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS
The statutory and constitutional duty to hold unlawful
agency action void is essential for securing civil liberties.
The establishment of administrative agencies altered the
nation’s constitutional structures in ways that eroded
both the Constitution’s structural freedoms and its enumerated rights. Accordingly , if administrative agencies
are to enjoy legitimacy , they must be subject to a sort of
judicial review that gives full effect to judicial findings
that agency action is unlawful.
Agencies enjoy the advantages of exercising the government’s tripartite powers. They regulate with their own
rules and adjudicate their own enforcement prosecutions.
Americans therefore need an effective mechanism to limit
unlawful agency action, and the APA attempted to legitimize the administrative state by providing such a mechanism, basing it on the traditional duty of judges to set
aside lower court judgments to the extent they are unlawful. The power of agencies to engage in rulemaking was
premised on this understanding that reviewing judges
would formally vacate agency action to the extent they
deemed it unlawful. It is therefore worrisome that the Solicitor General is asking this Court to weaken the APA ’s
judicial-oversight mechanism by misreading it as a declaratory or injunctive remedy directed at parties.
The Solicitor General’s position would cast aside both
the APA ’s judicial model of agencies and the APA ’s judicial
review of agencies as if they were lower courts. His position confuses supervisory action against lower courts with

24
equitable remedies against parties. It defies the history of
appellate review statutes, which dropped the word “enjoin” familiar from district court review and authorized
circuit courts merely to “set aside” agency action. It denies the constitutional power and duty of judges to set
aside lower court or agency action to the extent it is unlawful. It cuts off a crucial mechanism for preserving constitutional freedoms. And it undermines what little legitimacy was established for administrative agencies by subjecting them to the supervisory power of appellate courts.
CONCLUSION
The Court should reject the Solicitor General’s proposed interpretation of “set aside” in Section 706 of the
APA.
